target_only_tests.note: Thirteen target-only tests, translating NO interlock node id and NEVER counted as ported coverage. Two are seam liveness (rulebook rule 5: a seam a refactor stopped routing through would leave every case that replaces it green, because the replacement is simply never reached and the assertions -- which are about refusals -- still hold for the wrong reason). Two are continuo's expression of interlock#71's canary acceptance, which interlock#74 AC4 requires the port to carry rather than drop: interlock states the obligation as "the fencing spawn precondition is wired into the production spawn path", and in a module graph that is asserted, not asserted about -- one case drives every brokenness class through the production entry point and shows the spawner is never invoked, the other pins that src/fencing/spawn.ts imports the renderer and the battery as VALUES rather than as types, so a type-only import (which erases at compile time and would silently unwire the precondition) fails. See DECISIONS.md D-0205. Six more were added by D-0211, and they exist because the property cannot be written in TypeScript: a JSON number's Python spelling is recorded on its container slot (D-0210), the JavaScript literal `1.0` IS `1`, and so a case that built a role body in code carries no spelling into the document and passes against a renderer that has lost it. They serialise the shipped document, patch the numeric literals in as TEXT, read it back through `loadDocument`, drive `FencedSpawner.spawn`, and assert on the BYTES of the written `settings.local.json` and the published fence -- which is where D-0210's repair had stopped one call short. Interlock has no equivalent case because CPython has no equivalent defect: `json.loads` simply keeps the type. The fourth covers `pyDict`'s OTHER rebuild branch -- a sequence of pairs, where the value arrives as element 1 of the pair and its spelling was recorded on the pair rather than on the mapping being built. That branch is not reachable from `FencedSpawner` (a rendered fence always carries an object) but `Fence`, `fenceToJson` and `writeFence` are exported, which is where `pyDict`'s own note says its divergences live; `state.ts` writes the persisted fence through it. The fifth pins the TYPE-NAME half of the same root-slot boundary: a number at a document root has no container to hang a spelling on, so `pyTypeName` guesses, and the guess has to be the DOCUMENT's rule (CPython's syntactic one: no `.`, `e` or `E` makes it an int) rather than the serialiser's `pyNumberKind` -- which classifies values built in code and calls `-0` and anything past 2**53 a float. It also asserts the residue in BOTH directions: an integral float at a root reads `int` here and `float` in CPython, while the same document inside a container reads `float` on both sides. Reached through `FenceLedger.refusals()`, which persists `'<type>' object is not subscriptable`. The sixth covers `FenceLedger.append`, which builds its entry as `{event, at, ...payload}` -- a SPREAD is a rebuild, and it is the only one of the seven on the live spawn path. Without the carry a caller handing it a document-derived payload got the numbers re-spelled by JavaScript (`{"at": 1.0, "big": 9007199254740993}` written as `{"at": 1, "big": 9007199254740992.0}`). The case asserts both halves in one place because they interact: the record is built as ONE map rather than as a carry followed by the `PY_FLOAT` assertion, since `rememberNumberSpellings` REPLACES the record and asserting `at` after carrying would drop everything carried. See DECISIONS.md D-0211. Three more were added by D-0212, which audited the rebuild-site enumeration itself rather than trusting it: it swept `src/fencing` mechanically for container rebuilds and found that D-0211's list was complete as a list of sites that MUST carry, but that one rebuild branch had never been named at all -- `pyIterate`'s array branch, which returns `[...value]` and drops the index-keyed record like any other rebuild. It is left uncarried ON PURPOSE: `pysemantics` is not on the package surface, so its consumers are exactly the seven call sites in this subsystem and none of their results reaches `pyJsonDumps` or `pyTypeNameOf`; and adding the carry would ARM the stale-record trap rather than close one, because a caller may reorder the copy (`renderer.ts` sorts it) and an index-keyed record does not survive reordering. What stands in for a carry is therefore a proof, and these three cases are what keep that proof from being merely a sentence: the first MEASURES the drop (`pyJsonDumps(pyIterate(pyJsonLoads('[1.0, 9007199254740993]')))` is `[1, 9007199254740992.0]` where CPython's `json.dumps(list(x))` is `[1.0, 9007199254740993]`, because there the spelling lives in the VALUE and `list()` cannot lose it), so a future carry is a deliberate change rather than a silent one; the second and third pin the proof's two premises -- the call-site set, and the absence of `pysemantics` from `src/index.ts` -- each of which fails loudly when it stops holding. This is the difference between `pyIterate` and `pyDict`, which D-0211 HAD to repair even though `FencedSpawner` never reaches its pair branch, because `Fence`, `fenceToJson` and `writeFence` are exported and no call-site enumeration bounds a caller outside this repository. D-0212 also corrected the enumeration in the header of `src/fencing/pyjson.ts`, which named six branches and omitted `FenceLedger.append` -- the seventh, which D-0211's own entry and the case above had already counted. See DECISIONS.md D-0212. Five more were added by D-0095, the last inherited item of suisya-systems/continuo#18, and they cover the doors a document number leaves by that are NOT `json.dumps`: `role_kind` and `permission_mode` are converted with `str()` and land in wire fields the restart check compares; the settings payload's `permissionMode` is the RAW authored value copied out of a container whose slot `stripMeta` had already removed, so no rebuild carry could have reached it; and a refusal detail names the value through `repr()`. They are built the same way the D-0211 six are, and for the same reason -- the literals arrive as document TEXT -- and they assert on the BYTES of the published fence and `settings.local.json`. One of them covers the non-finite spelling, which is the one place `str()`/`repr()` and `json.dumps` are different CPython primitives (`inf` against `Infinity`): a role document spelling `"role_kind": 1e400` persisted `"Infinity"` here and `"inf"` in interlock. Not counted here, because it is not in this file: both entry points are also pinned against CPython by the differential vector (`pyjson.number_documents` gains a `texts` row beside its `types` row). The fifth is the READ side: `readFence` parses with `pyJsonLoads`, so a hand-edited fence's numbers can be named as the FILE spells them, and three refusals in `state.ts` were naming JavaScript's rendering instead. See DECISIONS.md D-0095.

approved_non_running.reason: Three capability gates on the file's real-child group (D-0081, continuo #119 / #120; D-0082, continuo #130). Unlike every other 'real provider' case in this suite, which drives a fake CLI, these three start an actual `claude -p`: they need a `claude` on PATH that is authenticated and can reach the API, and they bill a real turn. So the condition is `process.env.CONTINUO_REAL_CLAUDE_CHILD === "1" && claudeOnPath()`, probed once at module load exactly as pytest evaluates a skipif condition at collection time -- an environment variable AND the binary, because either alone would turn a machine without the other into a failing run rather than a skipped case. Nothing is lost when they are skipped that the file does not otherwise prove: the always-running cases pin the rendered mode, the deny rules' byte-identity, the `--setting-sources ''` pair in the plan's argv, and (D-0082) that the rendered sandbox block arrives switched on, spelled in strings and carrying the derived git roots. What only a child can show is that the CLI HONOURS them, which is precisely what both defects turned on -- the fence said something the CLI did not do -- so the cases exist and are run deliberately rather than being left unwritten. Observed green on 2026-09-04 against CLI 2.1.260 with the variable set: the hermetic case's witness file absent and the child's file written; the reproduction case's witness present and nothing written. D-0082 added the third gate for the same reason and one more: whether the CLI BUILDS the sandbox the fence declares is not observable from outside the child at all, so that case asks the child and reads the commit out of the repository afterwards rather than out of the child's account of itself. Observed green on 2026-09-04 against CLI 2.1.260 with the variable set: a `claude -p` in a real linked worktree staged and committed with no prompt and reported `SANDBOX YES`; the same fence before the repair reported no sandbox and could not stage. D-0093 (continuo #131) adds the fourth and fifth gates as one PAIR, and the pair is the point: the positive half asks a real child to `cat` a file at a path the worker role's `denyRead` covers and asserts the planted nonce does NOT reach stdout and that the refusal names `sandbox-deny-read`; the reproduction half re-spells that one entry `{"path": ...}` by hand in the settings file the plan already wrote and asserts the SAME read goes through and the nonce arrives. Measured on CLI 2.1.261, one non-string entry in `sandbox.filesystem.denyRead` or `denyWrite` makes the CLI apply neither `permissions.deny` nor any `PreToolUse` hook for the run, so without the reproduction half the positive half would be green whether the deny fired or the whole fence was void -- which is the failure mode D-0093 exists to record, written into the case rather than only into the entry. Observed green on 2026-09-06 against CLI 2.1.261 with the variable set, both halves. A first attempt planted the nonce OUTSIDE the worktree and proved nothing in either direction: the CLI's own working-directory guard refuses such a `cat` before the fence is consulted at all.

entries.reason: ADAPTED per D-0206. The source pins that the spawner callback runs OUTSIDE the ledger's cross-process lock: `FenceLedger.transaction` takes an exclusive `fcntl.flock` on a `.lock` sibling, and holding it for the duration of a blocking `claude -p` child would block every other role -- including one trying to record a REFUSAL, which interlock's own comment says must never wait. continuo takes no cross-process lock on any platform (D-0206: Node has no `flock` in core, and a hand-written `O_EXCL` lockfile converts a narrow window into a permanent deadlock on the fail-closed path), so it runs interlock's own `fcntl is None` branch -- the behaviour interlock itself ships on Windows. What the ported case pins is therefore the weaker but still load-bearing half that branch also has, and it pins it exactly as the source does: a second `FencedSpawner` is constructed, spawned and RECORDS its own refusal from INSIDE the first one's spawner callback. If the admission path ever grew a re-entrant in-process lock, or the child were moved inside the transaction, this deadlocks or fails to record, which is the source's failure too. Weaker than the source in the cross-process dimension and no weaker in any other; recorded here rather than left for a later reader to rediscover while wondering why nothing broke.

entries.reason: `monkeypatch.setattr(FencedSpawner, "_write_settings", boom)` patches the CLASS, so an instance built before the patch is affected too -- ordering the source relies on and the port keeps. The port patches `FencedSpawner.prototype.writeSettings` with `patchSeam` (D-0101 exports the method `@internal` for exactly this; `patchSeam` supplies monkeypatch's snapshot-at-patch and LIFO restore rather than a file-level undo, rulebook rule 5). One thing had to be ADDED rather than translated: the thrown error carries an errno-style `code` (`ENOSPC`). Node has no `OSError` class, so `isOSError` in src/fencing/spawn.ts classifies a filesystem failure by the string `code` Node puts on it -- a plain `Error` would escape the publication catch and fail the case with a raw throw instead of exercising the refusal path the source exercises. Every assertion of the source is kept, including `spawner.calls == []`, which is the one that says the child never started (D-0205).

inherited_limitations.topic: The ledger's `at`, the fence and the settings file are byte-identical to interlock's; what remains of the number contract is a scalar-rooted document and the rounded VALUE past 2**53.
inherited_limitations.status: REPAIRED (D-0210, completed by D-0211, and the `pyStr` residue this entry named closed by D-0095). This entry is the measurement, and the residue it names is what is still not carried.
inherited_limitations.detail: This entry previously disclosed a divergence: `FenceLedger.append` records `at` from the injected clock, `time.time()` is a float in Python and JavaScript has one number type, so interlock wrote `"at": 0.0` and continuo wrote `"at": 0`. It was the ONLY field in which a continuo ledger line differed from interlock's for the same inputs. D-0210 repairs it: `pyJsonLoads` now records each number's source spelling on its container slot and `FenceLedger.append` asserts `PY_FLOAT` for the clock's value, which is built in code and has no document behind it. MEASURED rather than argued: interlock's `FencedSpawner.spawn` and continuo's were both driven to an admission over the shipped role document, with the same context paths, the same `python`, the same hook file and the clock pinned to the same value, and all three artefacts -- `fence-worker.json`, `settings.local.json` and `fence-ledger.jsonl` -- compared EQUAL under `cmp` at clocks 0.0, 1700000000.0, 1700000000.5 and 1700000000.125. With the assertion removed the ledger diverges again in exactly one place (`"at": 0` against `"at": 0.0`) and the other two artefacts stay equal, which is the control that says the repair is what closed it. WHAT REMAINS, so the narrower claim above stays true: (1) `pyStr` still renders an integral float as an int, visible only for a role document that spells `role_kind` or `permission_mode` as a number -- no interlock role document does, and the six call sites do not all have a container to take a spelling from (see the note on `pyStr` in src/fencing/pysemantics.ts); (2) a number at the ROOT of a document has no container slot to hang a spelling on, so `pyJsonLoads("1.0")` still dumps as `1` -- every fencing artefact has an object at its root, and the one place a scalar root is reachable is a corrupt ledger line, whose `'float' object is not subscriptable` would read `'int'` here; (3) an integer past 2**53 keeps its exact DIGITS for re-emission but not its exact VALUE, which is still the rounded double. All three are stated in the header of src/fencing/pyjson.ts and pinned, where they are pinnable, by `pyjson.number_documents` in the differential corpus. CORRECTION (D-0211): the measurement above is sound and it was NOT sufficient, and the gap it left is worth recording next to it. It drove the SHIPPED role document, which carries no number in `env`, `permissions`, `sandbox` or `hooks`, so every artefact it compared was byte-equal whether or not the renderer carried the number record past `deepSortKeys` -- and `deepSortKeys` is the last call `settingsPayload` makes before the result becomes `fence.settings`. D-0210 therefore shipped with `settings.local.json` and the persisted fence still diverging for any document that put a number in a settings section (`"env": {"A": 1.0}` rendered `1`), while the artefacts this measurement compared stayed equal. D-0211 carries the record at that site and at a fifth one (`settingsPayload` itself), and pins both with target-only cases that assert on the written bytes; the residue listed above is unchanged. The transferable point is that a differential measurement is bounded by the inputs it is run over, and these inputs could not express the property the repair was about. Residue (2) is narrowed by D-0211 rather than removed: a root number's TYPE NAME is now answered by CPython's syntactic literal rule (no `.`, `e` or `E` is an int) instead of by the serialiser's value-based fallback, which had reported `9007199254740992` and `-0` as `float` where CPython says `int`. What remains at a root is only the integral float -- `1.0` and `1e16` read `int` here, `float` in CPython -- and that is asserted in both directions by a target-only case, together with the control that the same document inside a container answers correctly on both sides. CORRECTION (D-0095): residue (1) above is no longer residue, and the topic line is amended with it. `pyStr` took the document's spelling in the same shape `pyTypeName` already had -- an optional `PyNumberSpelling` plus a container-and-key `pyStrOf` beside `pyTypeNameOf` -- so `"role_kind": 1.0` now persists `"1.0"`, `9007199254740993` persists its digits, and `1e400` persists `"inf"` rather than JavaScript's `"Infinity"`. The claim that "the six call sites do not all have a container to take a spelling from" was measured again and did not hold: five of them do (the two `state.ts` reads take theirs from the payload `pyJsonLoads` returned, which is the persisted file's own spelling and exactly the right answer for a round trip), and the sixth (`FenceContext.mapping`) is typed `string`. D-0095 also found a defect this entry did not name at all, in the same field: `settingsPayload` copies the RAW `permission_mode` into the payload, and because `permission_mode` is a META key its slot is gone from `rendered` before the payload is built -- so `settings.local.json` wrote `"permissionMode": 1` where CPython writes `1.0`, and no rebuild carry could have reached it. Residues (2) and (3) are unchanged and are the runtime boundary. See DECISIONS.md D-0095.

inherited_limitations.topic: No `.lock` sibling of the ledger file is ever created.
inherited_limitations.detail: interlock's `FenceLedger.transaction` takes an exclusive `fcntl.flock` on `<ledger>.lock`, and degrades to the in-process lock alone where `fcntl` is unavailable -- which is the path it runs in production on Windows. Node has no `flock` in core on any platform, so continuo takes that same degraded branch everywhere (D-0206), and the visible artefact is that the `.lock` file no longer appears beside the ledger. What is lost is exactly one thing: two continuo processes publishing a fence to the SAME path concurrently can interleave their publish-then-record sequences. Each ledger LINE is still atomic (one `O_APPEND` write), within one process nothing is lost at all (every call on the path is synchronous), and publication of the fence file itself is a temp-sibling write plus `rename` and is unaffected. No case in the ported file asserts on the ledger DIRECTORY's contents -- the closest, `test_the_ledger_is_append_only`, reads the ledger FILE -- so no translated assertion depends on the difference. A hand-written `O_EXCL` lockfile was rejected on the record: `flock` is released by the kernel when the holder dies and a lockfile is not, so a SIGKILLed spawner would leave a stale lock blocking every later process, and the operation it blocks is the recording of a refusal, which must never wait. The option to reopen, if multi-process publication to one ledger ever becomes real, is a native binding.

inherited_limitations.topic: The text of a publication failure's refusal reason is Node's error message, not CPython's `str(OSError)`.
inherited_limitations.status: adapted message text (D-0017); the refusal CODE is identical
inherited_limitations.detail: src/fencing/spawn.ts formats a failed publication as `cannot publish fence: ${describe(exc)}` where `describe` is the transcription of CPython's `str(exc)` -- which never prefixes the class name. The message it wraps is the RUNTIME's, so a real ENOSPC reads `ENOSPC: no space left on device, open '<path>'` here where interlock reads `[Errno 28] No space left on device: '<path>'`. D-0017 governs: the refusal reason CODE (`RefusalReason.DOCUMENT_UNREADABLE`) and the sentence the port author writes are parity surface; the operating system's own sentence inside it is not, because no faithful translation of it exists. The two ported cases that reach this path assert on the outcome, the untouched filesystem and the recorded refusal rather than on the wrapped text, so nothing in the suite depends on the difference; a case that matched the message would be matching the platform.
